newsitem.title: USA: US bond mkt selloff seen aiding refunding auctions.
newsitem.headline: US bond mkt selloff seen aiding refunding auctions.

text.p: The latest U.S. Treasury market selloff last Friday may prompt greater demand for the Treasury's refunding, particularly for the 10-year and 30-year traches, market players said.
Over the next three days, the Treasury will sell $38.0 billion in three- and 10-year notes, and 30-year bonds in its quarterly refunding effort.
Early last week, many traders had wondered how well Wall Street could take down the upcoming supply with yields at their lowest levels in a year and a half.

But Treasury yields soared about 20 basis points over the past two sessions as prices swooned following a double dose of strong economic data on Friday. Traders said they now felt better about prospects for the auctions, particularly the 10-year and 30-year traches.

"The market is still somewhat expensive," said Scott Graham, co-head government bond trader at Prudential Securities Inc. "But it will be a lot easier to do 10s and bonds here than at Friday morning's levels."

On Wednesday, after the Treasury announced the details of the refudning, the when-issued three-year note traded at 5.85 percent, the when-issued 10-year note stood at 6.04 percent and the when-issued 30-year bond was at 6.29 percent.

Following Friday's selloff, which continued into Monday, those issues have jumped to 6.03 percent, 6.22 percent and 6.47 percent, respectively, with projections of rates rising another five or so basis points by the start of the three-day auctions on Tuesday.
"Clearly, now is a decent buying opportunity," said Graham.
"Three or four months down the road people will be happy they bought at these levels," he said.
Analysts said it was no accident Treasuries fell so sharply on Friday. They doubted that the data would have produced such a violent reaction with no auctions in sight.

"It was an excuse to take profits; it was an excuse to set up for the refunding," said Mike Cloherty, money market economist at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp. "I still think we have the fundamental story of low inflation ... but the (employment and National Association of Purchasing Management reports) were the first set of bad (bond market) news in a long time and the timing was sensitive."
The only wild card analysts said, was that the refunding precedes next week's retail sales report, which some see as more important to the market than the monthly employment data.
If strong July auto sales are any guide, retail sales could come in above the 0.4-percent gain currently expected, and that could send Treasuries tumbling further, traders warned.
"If there is concern longer term, people will wait (and not buy at the auction)," said Liz Miller, portfolio manager at Trevor Stewart Burton & Jacobsen Inc.
